properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony's idea, 2026-08-10, in his words: *"several times, I have had a brainstorming idea, and you've searched what I've already had in the graph. can we keep track of those searches for what's related because that tells you — the user had asked about something (or something similar or related) 10 times now... this node that has been searched 10 times now is becoming critical based on how many times it has been searched."*

REFINED BY HIM MINUTES LATER, and the refinement is right: *"instead of just keeping a simple integer counter, maybe relevance should also be included? for example, 5 other proposed ideas/decisions come up, but 2 of them were only 0.1 relevant, one was 0.4 relevant, and 2 were 0.8 relevant. then the critical decision path is weighted more towards the 0.8 relevant ideas versus the 0.1 ideas."* A count treats a barely-matching hit and a bullseye as the same event, and the tail of a ranked list is mostly noise — so an unweighted counter would be dominated by whatever happens to match loosely and often.

🛑 BUT THE SCORE THE SEARCH RETURNS IS NOT THE 0-TO-1 RELEVANCE THE IDEA ASSUMES, AND THIS IS THE CRUX. `search_design` is BM25, whose scores are UNBOUNDED and QUERY-DEPENDENT. MEASURED 2026-08-10, two queries about the SAME SUBJECT:

    query "export"                                                    top score   4.48
    query "the committed export document lineage content hash chain"  top score  35.75

EIGHT TIMES THE SCORE FOR THE SAME TOPIC, because BM25 rises with the number of matching terms. Accumulating raw scores would therefore weight a verbose query roughly eight times a terse one about the same thing, and would silently reward whoever writes longer queries. THERE IS NO 0.8 IN THE SYSTEM TODAY — the numbers look like relevances and are not.

⇒ THREE WAYS TO GET A COMPARABLE NUMBER, none chosen:
  (i) NORMALISE PER QUERY — divide by that result set's top score, giving 0-1 within one search. Cheap, available now, and it makes the two queries above agree. Costs the absolute signal: the top hit of a hopeless query scores 1.0 exactly like the top hit of a perfect one.
  (ii) RANK-BASED WEIGHT — reciprocal rank (1, 1/2, 1/3...), ignoring the score entirely. Immune to query length and to BM25's quirks; the standard trick for fusing incomparable rankings. Costs the distinction between a result set with one obvious winner and one with five near-ties.
  (iii) COSINE SIMILARITY FROM EMBEDDINGS — genuinely bounded, genuinely comparable across queries, and the only one of the three that actually delivers the 0.1/0.4/0.8 the idea describes. ⚠️ THIS MAKES THE IDEA A DEPENDENT OF AN ALREADY-OPEN QUESTION: `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` ("should reflow2 adopt embeddings and the HNSW index, or stay on lexical search?"). Worth naming plainly — if relevance-weighting is wanted in the form Anthony described, that decision has to be made first, and this is a new argument for it that the embeddings node does not yet carry.

OBSERVED IN THE SESSION THAT PRODUCED THE IDEA, which is why it is worth taking seriously rather than filing as a nice thought. Across roughly eight `search_design` calls on 2026-08-10, the same nodes kept surfacing unprompted: `fact:bl-198` twice, `dec:orientation-is-computed-not-written` twice, `dec:read-hint-shape` twice, and `cap:what-next` / `req:what-next` at the exact moment a new idea turned out to duplicate accepted intent. Each of those repeats CHANGED THE WORK — one of them stopped a false claim being shipped for the second time in three days. The signal is real in at least one session.

⚠️⚠️ IT COLLIDES WITH A LINE ANTHONY HIMSELF DREW, AND THE DISTINCTION IS PART OF THE VALUE OF THIS NODE. `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` says, verbatim: *"A SEARCH QUERY is content and is the worst offender, because it names the user's domain in their own words."* Read carelessly, that kills this idea. Read properly, it does not — because that requirement's scope is stated in its first line: *"WHEN REFLOW2 REPORTS ITS OWN USAGE FROM A HOSTED DEPLOYMENT."* It governs what LEAVES a design. This idea keeps the search history INSIDE the design it came from, where the object is not a leak but the entire point. SAME DATA, OPPOSITE DIRECTION. That distinction must be written down here, because a later session that finds this idea and remembers the telemetry rule will otherwise kill it correctly-looking and wrongly — or implement it and breach the rule by exporting it.

⇒ THE DERIVED CONSTRAINT, if this is ever built: search history is LOCAL BY CONSTRUCTION and never enters the telemetry payload. `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content`'s own argument applies — a structure that CANNOT carry content beats a policy promising not to — so the two must not share a transport.

`dec:how-should-reflow2-log-its-own-usage` IS ALREADY OPEN and holds the mechanism-and-storage question for usage logging. This idea widens what that decision has to answer: not only WHICH TOOLS a session called, but WHICH NODES it reached and HOW STRONGLY. Nodes are a harder case than tool names, exactly per the rule above.

TWO CONFOUNDS, BOTH SERIOUS, BOTH MEASURABLE BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING.

FIRST: A SEARCH HIT MEASURES THE AGENT'S QUERY WORDING AS MUCH AS THE USER'S INTEREST. Anthony did not run those eight searches — I did, choosing the words. A count would partly measure how I phrase things, and would drift as agents or models change. What he actually described is narrower and better: *the user had asked about something similar ten times*, which is a fact about HIS repeated approach to a topic, not about search mechanics. NOTE THAT WEIGHTING MAKES THIS CONFOUND WORSE, NOT BETTER, UNDER RAW BM25 — a longer agent query scores everything higher.

SECOND, AND SHARPER: SEARCH IS BM25 OVER NODE TEXT, SO A VERBOSE NODE WINS MORE SEARCHES. The nodes in this design are extremely verbose — several run to thousands of characters — and length is a scoring advantage in BM25. "Searched often" may therefore partly measure PROSE VOLUME rather than importance, and the verbose nodes are disproportionately the recent ones. That is testable directly: correlate hit frequency against node text length before trusting any of it. Per-query normalisation does NOT fix this one; it is a property of the corpus, not of the query.

AND A THIRD, SEEN TWICE TODAY: THE ONE-WORD "export" SEARCH RETURNED A `decision:ack:` REVIEW RECORD AS ITS TOP HIT. Whatever exclusion list a projection carries (`fact:graph-analysis-covers-a-third-of-the-edge-types`) applies here too — review records and bookkeeping must not accumulate attention weight.

AND `dec:bl-155`'S TRAP APPLIES ONE LEVEL OVER, unchanged. That decision found reflow2 cannot tell "unused" from "unreachable", and `req:telemetry-carries-usage-never-design-content` drew the consequence: usage counts may justify OPTIMISING and may not, alone, justify CUTTING. Here: SEARCH COUNTS MAY JUSTIFY RAISING SOMETHING AND MAY NOT JUSTIFY LOWERING WHAT IS NEVER FOUND — because you cannot search for what you do not know exists, and the nodes nobody finds are precisely the ones a discoverability problem hides.

THE OPTIONS.

(a) COUNT APPEARANCES IN SEARCH RESULTS, UNWEIGHTED. Cheapest. Counter: all three confounds hit it directly, and a result appearing in a list is not evidence anybody cared about it. Anthony's refinement is a direct argument against this one.

(b) COUNT ONLY WHAT WAS THEN READ IN FULL — a node that a search surfaced AND the agent then fetched with `get_node`. Much stronger evidence of relevance, and it discards the ranked-but-ignored tail where the BM25 confound lives. ⭐ NOTE THIS IS A RELEVANCE WEIGHT OF A DIFFERENT KIND — BEHAVIOURAL RATHER THAN LEXICAL — and it needs no score at all, so it sidesteps the comparability problem entirely. Counter: still an agent's behaviour, not the user's.

(c) RELEVANCE-WEIGHTED ACCUMULATION, per Anthony's refinement, using (i), (ii) or (iii) above. Closest to what he described. Counter: (i) and (ii) are approximations of the thing he means and (iii) depends on `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption`.

(d) RECORD THE SEARCH AS AN EVENT ATTACHED TO THE BRAINSTORM IT PRECEDED — "this idea was captured after searching X, and these nodes came back, at these ranks". A fact about the user's train of thought rather than about retrieval, and it composes with (c) since the weights ride on the event. Counter: covers only searches made during capture, and most searching is not.

(e) DO NOTHING; DERIVE IMPORTANCE FROM STRUCTURE INSTEAD. Measured the same day: 61 of 83 open decisions govern nothing, so structure currently has nothing to say about most of the pile — which is precisely the hole this idea would fill. Counter to the counter: that may be an argument for recording structure better rather than for measuring retrieval.

NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR EACH OTHER: this ranks by ATTENTION, `dec:idea-a-critical-path-through-the-undecided` ranks by CONSEQUENCE. A node can be repeatedly searched and block nothing, or block everything and never be searched. Whether either alone is enough, or they compose into one bounded top-5, is open in both nodes and settled in neither.
properties.name: OPEN — should repeated, RELEVANCE-WEIGHTED search hits mark a node as becoming critical, when BM25 scores are not comparable across queries and the same data is named "the worst offender" for telemetry?
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea, with his own refinement folded in the same session rather than minted as a third node — the refinement constrains the answer to this question, it is not a new question, and the complaint driving all of this is a pile of undecided nodes.

The load-bearing addition is that the refinement is RIGHT and CANNOT BE IMPLEMENTED AS DESCRIBED on the current search. Measuring two queries about the same subject and getting 4.48 against 35.75 is what turns "use the relevance score" from an implementation detail into a decision with a dependency: the 0.1/0.4/0.8 model needs a bounded similarity, which is what `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` is about. Recording that link is worth more than the idea itself, because a later session would otherwise reach for `score` believing it means relevance.

Option (b) is flagged because it dissolves the problem rather than solving it: what the agent chose to READ is a relevance signal that needs no score and cannot be gamed by query length.

The telemetry collision and the three confounds are kept with tests attached rather than as caveats. The BM25-length one is checkable in an afternoon and would decide whether any lexical weighting is worth having at all.
